new_statements.rule_in_words: Per Blust (whose Bintulu data are his own field data): stress is not contrastive; in citation forms stress falls on the final syllable, whose vowel is lengthened when word-final (lima [limá:], bivi [biví:], rəɗu [ʁəɗú:]); in connected speech the coastal-Sarawak pattern he describes is penultimate stress. Ghani 1992 p. 322 adds that full vowels can be 'long and stressed' (all her examples have the long stressed vowel in the final syllable) while schwa, including its final-syllable allophone [ʌ], is always short and unstressed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source opened.
new_statements.exceptions: Schwa never bears stress (Ghani 1992 p. 322: [ə] and final-syllable [ʌ] are 'short and unstressed'), so words with final schwa ([azʌŋ] 'large', [sepʌŋ] 'old') cannot be final-stressed. Blust's unpublished 1971 fieldnotes (RB2-003-D pp. 1-4) mark penult stress in many words with full-vowel penults ('lima, 'tuju?, 'supi?, 'pula, 'lupum) and final stress in others (bi'vi, sa'ba, ma'ta?, ja'bay, ki'ban), and carry his own query 'stress predictable?'; the 2013 [limá:] contradicts the 1971 'lima. The explicit rule sentence on p. 186 is a generalisation over coastal Sarawak languages, not a Bintulu-specific statement.
new_statements.domain_note: Citation forms (isolated words); Blust states that in phrasal context the same languages show penultimate stress, i.e. final stress marks decontextualised lexical data. Ghani 1992 describes 'standard' Bintulu of Kampung Masjid/Sebiew/Jepak etc; Blust's speaker is Umar bin Hamzah of Kampung Sebiew.
new_statements.identity_note: Bintulu = Vaie / Ba'ie (endonym; 'qaop ba?i' = Bintulu speech), a North Sarawak isolate of the Kemena basin around Bintulu town (Kampung Masjid, Sebiew, Jepak, Sibiew, Batu 10; upriver Pendan, Labang, Tubau; also Tatau, Sebauh, Niah). Not part of the Melanau chain (Blust 1988 per Ghani 1992). Ghani 1992 describes a 'standard' town variety; Blust's data (2013, fieldnotes) are from Umar bin Hamzah of Kampung Sebiew. Single glottocode bint1246; no dialect glottocodes.

sources.note: p. 186: stress is not phonemic in any language of Borneo; many coastal Sarawak languages have final stress in citation forms but penultimate stress in phrasal context. p. 265: word-final vowels predictably long in citation forms in several northern Sarawak languages, 'as in Bintulu ba [ba:] two, lima [limá:] five, bivi [biví:] mouth, or rəɗu [ʁəɗú:] female, woman' (final stress marked). p. 253: the same citation-form-final / phrasal-penult pattern is 'widespread in coastal and downriver areas of Sarawak'. Bintulu data are Blust's own field data (Blust n.d.(a)).

'wet', 'ñipən 'tooth'; final in tə'?go(o) 'thunder', pə'jin 'strong', ɣə?'du(u) 'woman', bi'vi(i) 'mouth', sa'ba(a) 'wife', tu'ba(a) 'fish poison', ma'ta? daw 'sun', ja'bay 'face', ki'ban 'forest', sa'kul 'hoe', lu'mis 'pale'. Not a published statement.

sources.note: Only pp. 321-322 are online (the Sarawak Museum's 'Download Abstract' PDF). p. 322 lists 23 consonants, 7 vowels, 5 diphthongs and describes each vowel: [i], [e], [a], [o], [u] are each 'also a long and stressed vowel' (examples with long final-syllable vowels: [si?ii] 'yesterday', [tu?aa?] 'hard', [uloon], [asuu?] 'plank'); schwa [e] 'is a short and unstressed vowel' and its allophone [^], 'limited to the final syllable of a word only', is 'short and unstressed'. No placement rule on the two pages. pp. 323-342 not accessible.
